channel.title: Road Guide: Lake Berryessa route
channel.description: Lake Berryessa: I-80 → I-505 → Winters → SR 128 → Rutherford → Calistoga → Alexander Valley → Healdsburg → Westside Rd. Play episodes in order as you drive.
channel.itunes:author: Wine Country Road Guide

item.title: 01. Welcome aboard: leaving the capital
item.description:
Good morning, and welcome aboard. I'll be your guide from the capital to the redwoods: across the floodplain, over the hills into Napa or Sonoma, and down to the Russian River at Guerneville. I'll chime in when there's something worth knowing, and keep quiet when there isn't. Tap the screen any time to see what I'm saying, or to skip me.
We're starting beside the Sacramento River, the reason this city exists at all. Sacramento grew up on the waterfront, because the river was the highway to the coast. Old Sacramento, the riverside historic district, still has its nineteenth-century brick build

item.title: 02. Sam Brannan, California's first millionaire
item.description: One name will follow us all day: Sam Brannan. He was a printer and a Mormon elder who sailed a shipload of Latter-day Saint emigrants round Cape Horn to California in 1846, bringing a printing press and a complete flour mill with him. He founded the California Star, San Francisco's first newspaper, and he's considered the first person to publicise the Gold Rush. His stores supplied the rush, and the profits made him California's first millionaire. He bought land everywhere, including a hot-springs valley at the far end of the Napa Valley that we may pass through later: he named it Calistoga.

item.title: 03. West Sacramento: the Town of Washington
item.description:
You've crossed into Yolo County and the city of West Sacramento. Its story begins with a widow. In 1849, James McDowell was shot dead in a bar argument he'd apparently started, leaving his wife Margaret with three daughters and 600 acres. She hired a surveyor, divided the land into forty-one blocks, and sold lots in a new settlement she called the Town of Washington. It became a rest stop for travellers struggling through the marshes towards Sacramento, and a busy fishing and farming centre, shipping salmon, sturgeon and crayfish as far as San Francisco.
Washington was later renamed Broderick

item.title: 04. The Yolo Bypass: a floodplain on purpose
item.description:
Look out at the flat land on both sides. You're on the Yolo Causeway, a three-mile viaduct across the Yolo Bypass, and this is one of the cleverest pieces of flood control in America. Rather than building ever-higher walls around Sacramento, engineers gave the river somewhere else to go.
Upstream, at a concrete spillway called the Fremont Weir, when the Sacramento River rises past a set height the excess simply pours over the top and into this basin. A second set of gates just north of West Sacramento can be opened by hand. In a big flood the bypass can carry several times the flow of the riv

item.title: 05. The causeway, the Tule Jake Road, and a quarter of a million bats
item.description:
Before any causeway, crossing this basin in the wet season meant a ferry, or a long detour south through Stockton. The first vehicle to make it across each summer set the line of the seasonal Tule Jake Road. The first causeway opened in 1916, a two-lane timber and concrete trestle, celebrated with a three-day party. In 1928 it was folded into the Lincoln Highway, the first road across America, and later carried Highway 40.
Today's twin structures date from 1962. Traffic reporters call them the long bridge and the short bridge. They're officially named for two Highway Patrol officers killed ne

item.title: 06. Davis: the university farm
item.description:
Coming up is Davis, a town that began as a railroad stop and became one of the most important agricultural universities on earth. The depot opened in 1868 and was named Davisville after Jerome C. Davis, a prominent local farmer. In 1907 the post office got tired of the extra syllables and shortened it to Davis.
In 1905 the state legislature passed the University Farm Bill, and Governor George Pardee chose Davis from about fifty candidate sites. Berkeley's agriculture dean, Eugene Hilgard, had admitted that Berkeley's foggy coastal climate was terrible for farming. The University Farm opened t

item.title: 07. Dixon: the town that moved to the tracks
item.description:
Dixon, coming up, is a town that literally picked itself up and moved. During the Gold Rush, a settlement called Silveyville grew up here as a halfway stop for miners heading between the coast and the Sacramento gold fields. When the railroad arrived in 1868, it missed Silveyville by a few miles. So in 1871 the townspeople relocated, buildings and all, to be next to the tracks. The Methodist church on North Jefferson Street is one of the buildings from that move.
The new town was supposed to be Dicksville, after Thomas Dickson, who donated ten acres for the depot. But in 1872 the first rail s

item.title: 08. Why the valley is so flat: seven miles of buried sea floor
item.description:
This is a geology story, and it starts with a question: why is the Sacramento Valley so astonishingly flat?
The answer is that you're driving across the top of an enormous filled-in basin. During the age of the dinosaurs, between about 150 and 65 million years ago, this whole valley was a seaway. To the east, where the Sierra Nevada stands now, ran a chain of volcanoes. To the west, an ocean plate was diving beneath North America, and the rocks scraped off it piled up into a ridge that acted like a dam. Between them lay a deep basin, and the volcanoes eroded into it, shedding mud and sand dow

item.title: 09. The Patwin: the people of this valley
item.description:
Before the farms, the freeway and the university, this western edge of the Sacramento Valley was home to the Patwin, the southern branch of the Wintun peoples, who have lived in this part of California since roughly the year 500.
The Patwin lived in settled villages, fishing, hunting and gathering, and acorns were central to life: across the plains and foothills, groves of oaks were a harvest. The southern Patwin lived between what is now Suisun, Vacaville and Putah Creek, and as Spanish and later settlers pushed in, they were broken into small groups whose names survive on today's map. The U

item.title: 10. The railroad that beat the Golden Spike
item.description:
If you've noticed a railway line running alongside the freeway, it has a sneaky claim to fame.
Everyone knows the transcontinental railroad was completed with a golden spike in May 1869. What's less known is that it ended at Sacramento, short of the Pacific. Getting trains on to San Francisco Bay was a separate race.
The tracks beside you were built by the California Pacific Railroad, incorporated in 1865 to link Vallejo, on the bay, with Sacramento. Its main line from Vallejo to Washington, today's West Sacramento, was finished in November 1868, six months before the golden spike. From Janu

item.title: 11. The Nut Tree: a fruit stand that fed a Queen
item.description:
Near the junction with Interstate 505 is the Nut Tree, now a shopping centre, once a California legend. It opened on the 3rd of July 1921 as a little roadside fruit stand on the Lincoln Highway, run by Helen and Ed Power. It was named after a black walnut tree that grew from a nut picked up on a trail in Arizona by a pioneer girl, Sallie Fox, before she arrived in Vacaville in 1859.
By its second year the stand was serving around 950 cars a day, and it kept growing as the old highway became Interstate 80: a restaurant with a floor-to-ceiling glass aviary, a bakery, a toy shop, its own little

item.title: 12. From the Lincoln Highway to Interstate 80
item.description:
The road you're on has been many roads. In 1913 the Lincoln Highway was dedicated: the brainchild of an Indiana entrepreneur, Carl Fisher, and one of the first highways in America designed for cars, running from Times Square in New York to Lincoln Park in San Francisco. At first its backers declined to shift it onto the new Yolo Causeway. But in 1928, after the Carquinez Bridge opened, the Lincoln Highway was rerouted over the Yolo Causeway and through Davis, Dixon, Vacaville and Fairfield, roughly where you are now.
When the federal numbered highways arrived, this became U.S. Highway 40. Roa

item.title: 13. Interstate 505: the highway that lost its letter
item.description:
You've turned north onto Interstate 505, a quiet four-lane spur that runs about thirty miles up the western edge of the Sacramento Valley to Interstate 5. It exists so that traffic between the Bay Area and the far north of California can bypass Sacramento entirely.
It has an odd backstory. It was originally planned as part of a looping interstate called I-5W, with a W for west. The federal highway authorities later scrapped almost all of those lettered interstates, so I-5W was chopped up and renumbered: part of it became I-580, part became the stretch of I-80 you just drove, and this part bec

item.title: 14. Winters: orchards on Putah Creek
item.description:
Winters, coming up, sits on Putah Creek where it leaves the hills, and it's one of the places where farming in the Sacramento Valley began.
In 1842, William Wolfskill, a Kentuckian who'd settled in Mexican California, was granted Rancho Rio de los Putos along the creek. His brother John started planting orchards and vineyards on the land, and is credited with beginning the agricultural development of the whole Sacramento Valley. The town came later: its post office opened in 1875, and it's named after Theodore Winters, whose ranch provided half of the town's land.
The Wolfskill connection la

item.title: 15. Putah Creek: the creek that came back
item.description:
The creek beside the road is Putah Creek, eighty-five miles long, from the Mayacamas Mountains to the Yolo Bypass. Its name has been argued over for a century and a half. Spanish-era records called it the Arroyo de los Putos, and for a while it was mapped as Puta Creek, until the federal naming board rejected that spelling, probably because of its resemblance to a rude Spanish word. The place-name scholar Erwin Gudde concluded the resemblance is purely accidental, and that the name comes from the Lake Miwok words for grassy creek. The Patwin name for it is Liwaito.
The creek has also been the

item.title: 16. Fire country on Highway 128
item.description:
These dry, grassy canyons burn often, and Highway 128 has been closed by fire again and again. In July 2015, the Wragg Fire started right beside the highway near Lake Berryessa, and the cause was mundane: the hot exhaust of an idling vehicle touching dry grass. It forced the evacuation of 136 homes and closed both this road and Interstate 505. In July 2017, the Winters Fire broke out a few miles south-west of Winters. In June 2020, the Quail Fire burned nearly 2,000 acres in Quail Canyon, between Winters and Vacaville.
Then, in August 2020, came the big one. A highly unusual series of thunder

item.title: 17. Monticello Dam and the Glory Hole
item.description:
Look up the canyon for Monticello Dam, a 304-foot concrete arch wedged into a narrow gorge known as Devil's Gate. It's a hundred feet thick at the base and just twelve at the top, and it was built between 1953 and 1957. When the last bucket of concrete was poured, on the 26th of February 1957, the crew followed tradition and tossed in a few coins.
The dam's claim to fame is its spillway, known as the Glory Hole. Instead of a channel over the side, there's a giant concrete funnel in the lake, 72 feet across at the lip, that drops 200 feet straight down through the hillside. When the lake is fu

item.title: 18. Monticello: the town under the lake
item.description:
Under Lake Berryessa lies a whole town. The valley was once Rancho Las Putas, granted in 1843 to two members of the Berryessa family, a prominent Californio family, which is where the lake gets its name. They lost much of it fast: by 1853 they were selling land to pay gambling debts, and when they couldn't pay a 1,645-dollar debt in cash, a creditor got the county to auction 26,000 acres. He bought it for 2,000 dollars and sold it for 100,000.
In 1866 developers laid out a town called Monticello. Farmers poured in, growing wheat and barley on what was considered some of the finest soil in the

item.title: 19. Who gets the water? The Solano Project
item.description:
California's history is in large part a history of moving water, and Lake Berryessa is a textbook case.
The farms of Solano and Yolo counties had been worked since the 1840s, but summer brought no reliable rain. As early as 1907, Bay Area cities hired three engineers, including George Washington Goethals and Arthur Powell Davis, to study damming Putah Creek; the result was known as the Mulholland-Goethals-Davis plan. The cities' interest moved on to bigger schemes. In the 1940s, Solano County's water council chose the Devil's Gate site, and in 1947 the county and the U.S. Bureau of Reclamatio

item.title: 20. Driving through tilted sea floor
item.description:
Now for some roadside geology, because the cuts along Highway 128 here are a slice through time.
The layered sandstones and shales you've been passing are the Great Valley Sequence, the same ancient sea-floor deposits that lie miles beneath the flat valley behind you. Here, on the valley's western margin, they come to the surface. On the Macrostrat geological maps, this canyon shows a run of named formations from the Late Cretaceous, the last age of the dinosaurs: the Sites, Venado and Yolo formations. The Venado is a massive greenish-grey sandstone, and near Monticello Dam its base includes

item.title: 21. Berryessa Snow Mountain: a monument without its lake
item.description:
The wild hills around Lake Berryessa are part of the Berryessa Snow Mountain National Monument, proclaimed by President Obama in July 2015 under the Antiquities Act. It stretches about a hundred miles north from here into Mendocino County, over 340,000 acres of the inner Coast Ranges, with bald and golden eagles, black bears, mountain lions and tule elk. These hills have been home to many Native peoples for around 11,000 years: Patwin, Pomo, Wappo, Lake Miwok, Yuki and others.
The politics are interesting. A broad coalition of counties, cities, the state legislature, a Pomo tribe and conserva

item.title: 22. Serpentine: the floor of an ancient ocean
item.description:
Watch the roadcuts and hillsides for a change in colour: greenish, shiny, slippery-looking rock and thin, scrubby vegetation. According to the Macrostrat maps, this stretch of Highway 128 crosses the Coast Range Ophiolite, and the rock here is serpentinised peridotite.
That's a remarkable thing to drive past. Peridotite is a dense rock derived from the Earth's mantle, rich in the green mineral olivine. An ophiolite is a section of ocean crust and the upper mantle beneath it that has been uplifted and pushed onto continental rocks. When sea water is forced deep into rock like this, it turns it

item.title: 23. The Franciscan Complex: California's geological junk drawer
item.description:
Much of the Coast Ranges, from here west to the ocean, is built of one of the strangest rock assemblages on Earth: the Franciscan Complex.
For tens of millions of years, from the Jurassic onward, an ocean plate dived beneath the edge of North America. As it went down, it scraped off a chaotic mixture of material: deep-sea sandstone called graywacke, chert containing the fossils of tiny radiolaria, basalt from the ocean floor, and slices of rock that had been dragged deep down and squeezed under enormous pressure before popping back up. Geologists call the mashed-up result an accretionary wedg

item.title: 24. Lake Hennessey and the valleys behind the hills
item.description:
The lake beside you now is Lake Hennessey, the City of Napa's main water supply. Congress authorised a dam here in 1944 to protect Napa from floods, but never paid for it, so in 1946 the city built Conn Creek Dam itself, for 550,000 dollars, plus thirty miles of pipe made by the Basalt Rock Company south of Napa. It's named after Edwin Hennessey, a local civic leader who helped develop it.
The name has a second meaning now. Early on the morning of the 17th of August 2020, a lightning-sparked spot fire was reported on Hennessey Ridge Road near this lake. The Hennessey Fire grew to 192,000 acre

item.title: 25. Rutherford: a sea captain, a Godfather and the sacramental wine
item.description:
Rutherford is named after Thomas Rutherford, who married one of George Yount's granddaughters. In 1864 Yount gave the couple about a thousand acres, and Rutherford planted it with vines.
The great estate here is Inglenook, founded in 1879 by Gustave Niebaum, a Finnish sea captain who'd made a fortune in the Alaska fur-seal trade and helped promote the Alaska Purchase. He'd wanted to build a winery in France, but his California-born wife disliked long ocean voyages, so Napa it was. Inglenook wines won gold medals at the 1889 Paris World's Fair. After decades of corporate ownership, the estate

item.title: 26. Oakville: To Kalon, Mondavi and Opus One
item.description:
Coming up is Oakville, population about fifty, and some of Napa's most famous Cabernet land. It started in the 1860s as a water stop for Brannan's steam train, named for the dense groves of valley oaks.
In 1868 a man called H. W. Crabb bought land near the river and planted a vineyard he named To Kalon, Greek for the beautiful. He experimented with over 400 grape varieties to find what suited the place, and by 1880 had 430 acres of vines. In 1903 the U.S. Department of Agriculture set up an experimental vineyard here, and the Oakville Station is run by UC Davis to this day.
In 1965, after a

item.title: 27. How the Napa Valley was built: volcanoes, faults and gravel
item.description:
Let's talk about the ground under all those vines, because in this valley the geology is the product.
Start with the shape. The Napa Valley is a long, narrow trough between two ranges, the Mayacamas on the west and the Vacas on the east. California's great fault system is about fifty miles wide here, a whole family of faults, including the West Napa Fault, slicing north-west through the region and slowly sliding the land past itself.
Then the volcanoes. In the late Miocene and Pliocene epochs, between about eleven and three million years ago, this area was volcanic. The result is the Sonoma

item.title: 28. The Wappo: the brave ones
item.description:
Long before vineyards, the upper Napa Valley was Wappo country. The Wappo homelands spread across the Napa Valley, the south shore of Clear Lake, the Alexander Valley and the Russian River valley. Their language belongs to the Yukian family, distantly related to the Yuki people further north.
They lived by hunting and gathering, in small, independent groups with no central authority, in homes of branches, leaves and mud. Their baskets were woven so tightly they could hold water. Oaks gave acorns, a staple food, and the hot springs at the head of the valley were a place of healing. There were

item.title: 29. Bust: phylloxera, Prohibition and the Depression
item.description:
By 1880, the Napa Valley was booming. There were 443 vineyards with a thousand or more vines each, most of them around St. Helena, and by the end of the century there were more than 140 wineries. Then came three blows in a row.
The first was tiny: phylloxera, a louse that attacks grapevine roots. It killed many of the vines throughout the valley. The answer, which Georges de Latour of Beaulieu helped bring in, was rootstock that resisted the pest.
The second was Prohibition, enacted in 1920. Many wineries simply shut down. A few survived by making sacramental wine for churches, and growers w

item.title: 30. The Judgment of Paris
item.description:
Here's the story that put this valley on the world map.
In the early 1970s, some California wines were outstanding, but hardly anyone noticed; the market wanted French labels. A British wine merchant in Paris, Steven Spurrier, who mainly sold French wine, organised a tasting with his American colleague Patricia Gallagher to mark America's bicentennial. On the 24th of May 1976, eleven judges, most of them French wine experts, tasted top Chardonnays and Cabernets blind, French against Californian, scoring each out of twenty. Spurrier expected the French to win.
They didn't. In both categories,

item.title: 31. St. Helena: Beringer, Krug and the castle of wine
item.description:
Welcome to St. Helena, the heart of the old Napa wine country. The town was founded in 1854 when two men bought a tract on the west side of Main Street from Maria Ignacia Bale, the widow of an English doctor we'll meet in a minute. It's likely named after the mountain to the north.
This is where the valley's wine industry put down roots. Charles Krug started his winery here in 1861; it's often cited as the valley's first. He married Dr. Bale's daughter, and her mother insisted on a prenuptial agreement protecting twenty acres of land north of town, where Krug planted his vines. Much later, in

item.title: 32. The happy accident of White Zinfandel
item.description:
On Highway 29 in St. Helena is Sutter Home, home of one of the great accidents in wine history. The winery dates to 1874, sat abandoned after Prohibition, and was bought in 1948 by the Trinchero brothers, who scraped by on jug wine.
In 1972, Bob Trinchero began making a pale wine from red Zinfandel grapes. Then, making the 1975 vintage, about a thousand gallons of the juice stopped fermenting before all the sugar was used up. He set it aside, tasted it two weeks later, and found it sweet, pink and, in his view, pretty good. They bottled it. By 1987 Sutter Home White Zinfandel was the best-sel

item.title: 33. The Bale Grist Mill and the redwoods of Bothe
item.description:
Watch for the Bale Grist Mill, just off the highway between St. Helena and Calistoga, with its 36-foot waterwheel. It's one of only two water-powered mills left west of the Mississippi.
It was built in 1846 by Dr. Edward Turner Bale, an English ship's surgeon who landed at Monterey in 1837, became surgeon-in-chief of the Mexican army under General Vallejo, and married Vallejo's niece. He was granted Rancho Carne Humana, all the land between today's Rutherford and Calistoga. The mill was finished the same year as the Bear Flag Revolt, and there's evidence the rebels met at Bale's mill before t

item.title: 34. Castles, cable cars and caves
item.description:
The approach to Calistoga has some of the valley's most theatrical wineries.
Castello di Amorosa is a full-scale medieval-style castle, opened in 2007 by the vintner Dario Sattui. It has 107 rooms on eight levels, a moat, a drawbridge, a great hall with frescoes and a torture chamber with an iron maiden he says he bought in Italy for 13,000 dollars. It was built from 8,000 tons of local stone and 850,000 bricks imported from Europe, on land once owned by Dr. Bale. In the 2020 Glass Fire, its farmhouse burned and a whole vintage was lost, but the castle came through unharmed.
Nearby, Sterling

item.title: 35. Calistoga: a slip of the tongue
item.description:
Welcome to Calistoga, at the head of the Napa Valley, and the town with the best origin story of the day.
It was Sam Brannan again, the Gold Rush millionaire. He visited the hot springs here in 1852, was fascinated, and bought more than 2,000 acres to build a spa to rival the fashionable Saratoga Springs in New York. The story goes that he meant to call it the Saratoga of California, but it came out as the Calistoga of Sarafornia. Whether that's literally true or Brannan just liked the tale, the name stuck. His resort opened in 1862, and his railroad arrived in 1868, bringing San Francisco's

item.title: 36. Robert Louis Stevenson's squatter honeymoon
item.description:
In 1880, a sickly, broke Scottish writer arrived in Calistoga with his new American wife. Robert Louis Stevenson had crossed an ocean and a continent to marry Fanny Vandegrift Osbourne, and friends suggested the mountain air of the upper Napa Valley might help his lungs.
They tried the Hot Springs Hotel, but couldn't afford ten dollars a week. So they spent a two-month honeymoon squatting, with Fanny's twelve-year-old son Lloyd, in an abandoned three-storey bunkhouse at a derelict silver mine called Silverado, high on the shoulder of Mount Saint Helena. They patched the windows with cloth, ha

item.title: 37. Mount Saint Helena and the Russian princess
item.description:
If you can see the big mountain to the north of Calistoga, that's Mount Saint Helena, the peak that closes off the head of the Napa Valley. It has five summits arranged in a rough letter M. The highest is in Sonoma County, and the next is the high point of Napa County. The Napa River starts on its slopes, and it's one of the few mountains in the Bay Area that gets snow in winter.
The Wappo called it Kanamota, Human Mountain. Spanish colonists called it Mount Mayacamas. The name it has now comes from an unexpected direction: Russia. In 1841, a Russian survey party from Fort Ross, on the Sonoma

item.title: 38. Wine country on fire: 2017, 2020, and the insurance crisis
item.description:
Driving through these hills, you'll see blackened trunks and new houses where old ones stood. This is the story of the fires.
On the night of Sunday the 8th of October 2017, hot, dry Diablo winds were gusting up to seventy miles an hour across Northern California. Over a dozen wildfires broke out that night. One started at 9:43 p.m. near Tubbs Lane, in the rural north of Calistoga. Pushed by north-easterly winds, the front of the Tubbs Fire moved more than twelve miles in its first three hours, through the Mark West Springs area and into the city of Santa Rosa. It destroyed more than 5,600 st

item.title: 39. Hot ground: the Sonoma Volcanics, Clear Lake and The Geysers
item.description:
You're crossing the Mayacamas Mountains, and almost everything around you was once molten.
The rock is called the Sonoma Volcanics: obsidian, pumice, tuff, rhyolite, andesite breccia and basalt lava, several thousand feet thick. It forms most of the mountains around the Napa and Sonoma valleys, and it probably once formed a continuous mass from San Pablo Bay north into Lake County, and from Solano County west to the Santa Rosa plain. Geologists think it erupted from several vents, on and off, over perhaps more than a million years, mostly in the Pliocene, three to five million years ago. It's

item.title: 40. Knights Valley: a Mexican soldier's hunting preserve
item.description:
Over the hill from Calistoga, Highway 128 drops into Knights Valley, a small, quiet valley about five miles long, with the warmest climate in Sonoma County.
In 1843 the Mexican governor rewarded a soldier from the Sonoma presidio, José de los Santos Berreyesa, with a grant of nearly 18,000 acres called Rancho Mallacomes, which took in this valley and even the hot springs at what's now Calistoga. Berreyesa kept the valley as his private hunting preserve, and the adobe hunting lodge he built still survives.
The valley's English name comes from Thomas Knight, a native of Maine who had taken par

item.title: 41. Chalk Hill: white volcanic ash in the vineyards
item.description:
The hills to the south-west are the Chalk Hill wine area, named after a prominent hill. The chalk isn't really chalk at all. It's white tuff, volcanic ash from the eruptions of the Mount Saint Helena area, the same volcanism that buried the Petrified Forest. That pale, ashy soil is said to suit white grapes like Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc. A warm thermal belt runs through the area, and harvest here often comes in September, weeks before the neighbouring regions.
A little further on, along Alexander Valley Road, the Macrostrat maps show a basalt flow of the Sonoma Volcanics and the Glen El

item.title: 42. Alexander Valley: Kit Carson's brother and the Wappo name
item.description:
You're entering the Alexander Valley, the broad, vine-filled valley of the Russian River north of Healdsburg. It's the largest and most fully cultivated wine region in Sonoma County, and stretches from the river east to the Mayacamas foothills, with more than a hundred wineries.
The story begins with a Mexican land grant, Rancho Sotoyome, almost 49,000 acres along the river, named after a Wappo group, the Satiyomes. It went to Henry Fitch, a San Diego sea captain who was General Vallejo's brother-in-law. Fitch never lived here. He hired a manager, Cyrus Alexander, under a four-year deal, afte

item.title: 43. Healdsburg: a squatter's town and the birthplace of lemon pepper
item.description:
Healdsburg sits on the Russian River where three famous wine regions meet: the Alexander Valley, the Dry Creek Valley and the Russian River Valley. The Pomo built villages in the open land along the river here.
The town is named after Harmon Heald, an Ohio businessman who squatted on Rancho Sotoyome from 1850. When the Fitch family auctioned off land to pay their taxes, he bought a piece in 1857, and the town was incorporated in 1867. The railroad arrived in 1872. For decades this was orchard country. When Prohibition shut down the wineries of the Dry Creek Valley, which had been one of Calif

item.title: 44. Isabelle Simi, a winery that outlasted Prohibition, and Lytton
item.description:
Healdsburg's Simi Winery was founded in San Francisco in 1876 by two Italian brothers who'd come for the Gold Rush, and moved here in 1881, buying a winery for 2,250 dollars in gold coin. From 1904 it was run by Giuseppe Simi's daughter, Isabelle, who kept making wine all through Prohibition and stored it in the stone cellars. When repeal came in 1933, Simi was one of the few companies with wine ready to sell. In 1973 the winery hired Maryann Graf, the first woman to graduate from an American university with a degree in winemaking.
Just north of town, Lytton has an extraordinary history in a

item.title: 45. Westside Road: blueschist and Pinot Noir
item.description:
Westside Road winds along the west bank of the Russian River, through some of the most celebrated Pinot Noir country in California. This is the heart of the Russian River Valley wine region, cool and foggy, where commercial wineries took off in the 1870s.
But look at the rocks too. The Macrostrat geological maps show this stretch crossing the Eastern Belt of the Franciscan Complex, including blueschist-facies metagraywacke: sea-floor sandstone that was carried down a subduction zone, squeezed at high pressure but relatively low temperature, and turned blue with the mineral glaucophane, before

item.title: 46. California's first commercial sawmill
item.description:
The land around Forestville and Mirabel was once Rancho El Molino, the Ranch of the Mill. It was granted in 1833 to John Bautista Rogers Cooper, a sea captain who'd married General Vallejo's sister. The grant had a strategic purpose: the Mexican authorities wanted settlers pushing west toward the coast to counter the Russian presence at Fort Ross.
In 1834 Cooper built a water-powered sawmill here, driven by Mark West Creek and cutting redwood. It's recognised as the first water-powered commercial sawmill in California. The river had the last word, though: floods destroyed it in the winter of

item.title: 47. Meeting the Russian River
item.description:
Welcome to the Russian River, the last leg of the journey. It's the second-largest river in the Bay Area after the Sacramento, with a main stem 115 miles long, flowing south from Mendocino County and then west to the Pacific.
It has had a lot of names. The Southern Pomo called it Ashokawna, east water place, and also Bidapte, big river. A Spanish land grant of 1843 called it the Rio Grande. Its current name comes from the Russian-American Company, which ran the fur-trading colony at Fort Ross on the coast in the early 1800s. A Russian explorer, Ivan Kuskov, travelled up the river, and an 1817

item.title: 48. The Pomo: the people of the Russian River
item.description:
The Russian River is Pomo country. The Pomo lands once stretched from the Pacific coast inland to Clear Lake, but the Pomo were never one nation. They lived in small, independent bands, linked by family and marriage, and spoke seven related languages so different that speakers of one couldn't understand another. Linguists think their ancestors may have reached the Clear Lake uplands thousands of years ago, and later spread into the Russian River valley.

item.title: 49. Floods, dams and the river that borrows from the Eel
item.description:
This lovely, lazy river has a violent side. Flood stage at Guerneville is 32 feet, and in the second half of the twentieth century the river topped it about five times a decade. The record is 49.5 feet, in February 1986. January 1995 hit 48 feet. Two big dams upstream, Coyote Valley Dam, built in 1959, forming Lake Mendocino, and Warm Springs Dam, finished in 1982, forming Lake Sonoma, now hold back some of the flood water, and flooding is less frequent. But in February 2019 the river rose to levels comparable to 1986.

item.title: 50. Korbel: Bohemian brothers and California champagne
item.description:
On the riverbank near Rio Nido is Korbel, which has made sparkling wine here since 1882. It was founded by Francis Korbel and his brothers, emigrants from Bohemia, who'd also founded a satirical San Francisco magazine called The Wasp. They used the traditional Champagne method, where the wine is fermented a second time in the very bottle you buy.

item.title: 51. Rio Nido: there is no Canyon Five
item.description:
Rio Nido, the river nest, is a little resort village tucked into a redwood canyon. In 1908 a San Francisco fraternal lodge, the Eagles, bought the land and divided it among members, and the place was first called Eaglenest. During the Second World War its dance hall heaved with sailors on liberty and troops heading for the Pacific, and big bands played there. A small excursion boat once ran down the river to Guerneville's beach.

item.title: 52. Guerneville: from Stumptown to resort town
item.description:
Welcome to Guerneville, and congratulations, you've made it. First, the name: it's said Gurn-vill, and locals sell T-shirts reading Don't call it Guerneyville, although people have been saying it that way since the 1800s.
The local Pomo used this spot as a summer camp and called it Ceola, the shady place. The redwoods here grew so thickly that local lore says the valley once had the greatest density of living matter on the planet. Then came the loggers. item.title: 53. Armstrong Redwoods: the trees the loggers missed
item.description:
Just north of town is Armstrong Redwoods State Natural Reserve, 805 acres of coast redwoods, including old-growth forest. In the 1870s, Colonel James Armstrong set the grove aside as a natural park. After his death his daughter and another local family campaigned with meetings, rallies and car caravans to save this last remnant of the old forest, and in 1917 Sonoma County bought it for 80,000 dollars.
